name: Guadalajara International Airport
before:
Mexico's third busiest airport, in Tlajomulco de Zúñiga about 17 km south east of downtown Guadalajara. It handled 18,696,600 passengers in 2025 and ranks ninth in Latin America.

It is the largest hub for Volaris and the airline's main gateway to the United States, as well as a hub for Viva and a focus city for Aeroméxico. Flights reach across Mexico, the Americas and Europe.

Two points of practical detail. The airport sits at 1,529 metres above sea level, and the single terminal is currently undergoing renovation, so expect building works. Two runways serve it, the longer at 4,000 metres.

It is officially named after Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, a leader of the Mexican War of Independence, and is operated by Grupo Aeroportuario del Pacífico.
after:
Mexico's third busiest airport, in Tlajomulco de Zúñiga about 17 km south of downtown Guadalajara. In 2025 it handled about 18.7 million passengers.

It is Volaris's largest hub and a major base for its flights to the United States. Aeroméxico also flies from here. Flights reach across Mexico and the rest of the Americas.

The airport sits at 1,529 metres above sea level. Two runways serve it, the longer at 4,000 metres. Its operator, Grupo Aeroportuario del Pacífico, plans a new terminal building in its 2025 to 2029 investment programme.

It is named after Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, a leader of the Mexican independence movement.

claims.note: GAP's own airport page is undated and parts of it are old (it says 'two terminals' and its airline page still lists Interjet), so the 2025 figures were checked as well: Guadalajara 18.7 million (GAP), behind Cancún, which ASUR's annual report of 16 April 2026 says was second in Mexico in 2025 on AFAC's figures, and ahead of Monterrey (15.6 million, OMA) and Tijuana (12.65 million, GAP). AFAC's own national table (gob.mx) is behind a bot check, so the Mexico City airports' 2025 figures were not read; the rank rests on Wikipedia's 2025 infobox and GAP's statement, with the operator figures consistent with it.

claims.wasBefore: as well as a hub for Viva
claims.why: Airline bases are time-sensitive and nothing from the last 12 months says Viva has a hub here. The newest reports found are Mexico Business News (2 August 2024, eight new Guadalajara routes) and SDP Noticias (4 June 2025, Viva dropping its Ciudad Obregón route); GAP's 2026 monthly releases list no new Viva routes from Guadalajara.
'Focus city' is Wikipedia's label only; softened to 'Aeroméxico also flies from here', which GAP and Aviacionline support.

claims.wasBefore: Flights reach across Mexico, the Americas and Europe.
claims.why: No current European route could be confirmed. Aeroméxico's page on its Guadalajara to Madrid flights shows only 'Site Maintenance'; the one European route found is Aeroméxico's Guadalajara to Paris from 13 April 2027 (Aviacionline, 7 September 2026), a single source, held back below.
Framing for the elevation and the building works; the works claim is replaced, so the lead-in goes.

claims.why: Wikipedia alone and undated; no source from the last 12 months describes works at the existing terminal. Replaced by the planned new terminal (GAP, September 2026). The terminal count is also disputed: GAP's own undated airport page says 'two terminals'.

claims.wasBefore: It is officially named after Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla
claims.why: 'Officially' rests on Wikipedia; GAP says 'also called'. The naming itself is kept.

Held back: Aeroméxico will fly Guadalajara to Paris Charles de Gaulle three times a week from 13 April 2027 (Aviacionline, 7 September 2026, reporting Aeroméxico's statement). One source; it would restore Europe to the text once a second (Aeroméxico's own release) is saved.

claims.why: Held back: after security events across Jalisco on 22 February 2026, 120 flights were cancelled at Guadalajara that day and 103 the next (GAP), and traffic fell in March. The FCDO's current advice (updated 22 September 2026) warns against all but essential travel only to parts of Jalisco south and south-west of Lake Chapala and some northern municipalities, not Guadalajara or Tlajomulco. The old text says nothing on security, so nothing to replace.
